cur:monumental2-lmbatavank-apse.summary: The apse conch preserves the lower half of a monumental theophany: the lower body and jewelled footstool of the enthroned Christ, radiating lines of glory, and, at the sides, fiery wheels and wings of the heavenly powers that surround him. The upper part with Christ's head has been lost, yet the painting remains one of the rare surviving 7th-century church murals in Armenia.
facts: Lmbatavank is a small cruciform domed church of the 7th century dedicated to Saint Stephen; its apse frescoes show 'Jesus in the center surrounded by symbols of heavenly powers'.
A painting of Saint George on horseback holding a cross-topped staff also survives in the church.
cur:monumental2-lmbatavank-apse.notes: Christ's figure survives only below the waist; identification of the theophany follows Wikipedia.

walters:37.525.summary: Among towering, vine-hung ruins of fluted Corinthian columns, a small figure of Christ in a pale robe raises his hand toward a group of mothers who press forward with their children, while bystanders in turbans and robes look on. The biblical scene is almost absorbed into the grandeur of the decaying classical architecture and the distant town. It is a typical capriccio of ruins in which a Gospel episode gives the landscape its meaning.
facts: Alberto Carlieri (Italian, 1672–after 1720) specialised in such architectural fantasies; the Walters dates the canvas to the first quarter of the 18th century.
When it was in the Massarenti collection in Rome, its 1897 catalogue attributed it to Bibiena; Henry Walters bought it with that collection in 1902.
walters:37.525.notes: The worklist year (900) was wrong; the painting is early 18th century. The Walters' period label 'Renaissance' is not apt, so the style is given as Baroque.

wga:zearly/1/2mural/2marcell/marcel11.summary: On the ceiling of a burial chamber, Christ sits enthroned at the centre, bearded and haloed, in a dark robe with an open book, while Peter and Paul stand on either side gesturing toward him. In the register below, the Lamb stands on a hill, and four martyrs of this catacomb, labelled with their names, approach in acclamation. The painting joins the heavenly court of Christ with the local saints venerated in this very place.
facts: The four martyrs below are named by painted inscriptions; the names of Gorgonius and Tiburtius can still be partly read, and the group is usually completed by Peter and Marcellinus, the martyrs after whom the catacomb is named.
The Lamb standing on a mount, the symbol of Christ sacrificed and victorious, is a motif that later reappears in the apse mosaics of Roman churches.

links.label: Wikipedia: Catacombs of Marcellinus and Peter

wga:zearly/1/2mural/2marcell/marcel11.notes: The identification of all four martyrs is based on the usual reading of this fresco; only parts of the inscriptions are legible in the photograph. Some scholars date the painting to the late 4th or early 5th century.

feat:batoni-sacred-heart-of-jesus.summary: Christ, in a red tunic and blue mantle, gazes gently at the viewer and holds out his radiant heart, encircled by thorns and crowned with a cross and flame. Pompeo Batoni painted the image in 1767, shortly after the papacy first approved a liturgical feast of the Sacred Heart; it is kept in the Jesuit mother church in Rome, the Gesù. Through countless prints and holy cards, it became one of the most widely reproduced images of Christ in the world.
facts: Devotion to the Sacred Heart spread from the visions of Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial, France (1673–75), and was championed by the Jesuits.
In 1765 Pope Clement XIII first approved a feast of the Sacred Heart, granted to particular petitioners rather than the whole Church; Batoni's painting followed two years later.
The painting first stood on the altar of the chapel of Saint Francis Xavier in the Gesù; in 1920 it was moved to the former chapel of Saint Francis of Assisi, rededicated to the Sacred Heart.

Batoni was the most sought-after portraitist in 18th-century Rome, famous for painting British aristocrats on the Grand Tour, and his soft, approachable Christ shaped popular Catholic iconography well into the 20th century.
